subQuestions.questionText: DNA differs from RNA in that DNA…
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — contains the sugar deoxyribose, while RNA contains ribose (2 marks)
DNA contains the pentose sugar deoxyribose, whereas RNA contains ribose. DNA has thymine (not uracil), DNA is double-stranded, and DNA is found mainly in the nucleus.

options.B: contains the sugar deoxyribose, while RNA contains ribose
options.C: is single-stranded, while RNA is double-stranded
options.D: is found only in the cytoplasm, while RNA is found only in the nucleus

subQuestions.questionText: During which phase of meiosis does crossing over take place?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — Prophase I (2 marks)
Crossing over (exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes) occurs during Prophase I of meiosis.

subQuestions.questionText: A normal human somatic cell contains 46 chromosomes. After meiosis is complete, each daughter cell will contain:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — 23 chromosomes (2 marks)
Meiosis halves the chromosome number from diploid (2n = 46) to haploid (n = 23).

subQuestions.questionText: If both parents have blood group AB, the possible blood groups of their children are:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — A, B and AB (2 marks)
AB × AB cross: gametes IA and IB from each parent give offspring IAIA (group A), IAIB (group AB), and IBIB (group B). No O is possible because neither parent carries the i allele.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following is the BEST evidence for evolution from a common ancestor?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — Homologous structures in different species (e.g. forelimbs of mammals) (2 marks)
Homologous structures share the same basic plan but have different functions, which is strong evidence of descent from a common ancestor with later modification by natural selection.

options.B: Homologous structures in different species (e.g. forelimbs of mammals)
options.C: Fossils being found mainly in sedimentary rock
options.D: All organisms having the same body temperature

subQuestions.questionText: Which of these features is characteristic of humans (and NOT of modern African apes)?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — S-shaped vertebral column (2 marks)
The S-shaped (curved) vertebral column is a key adaptation for upright bipedal posture in humans. Apes have prominent canines, long arms, and a foramen magnum at the back of the skull.

options.A: Foramen magnum positioned at the back of the skull
options.D: Long arms relative to the legs

subQuestions.questionText: Lamarck's theory of evolution differs from Darwin's theory in that Lamarck believed:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — Acquired characteristics during life can be inherited by offspring (2 marks)
Lamarck proposed that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime (through use and disuse) could be passed to offspring. This is now disproved by genetics — only changes to DNA in gametes are heritable.

options.A: Variation already exists in a population before selection acts
options.B: Acquired characteristics during life can be inherited by offspring
options.C: Natural selection favours the best-adapted individuals
options.D: Evolution occurs only through random mutation

subQuestions.questionText: Which process is NOT a form of asexual reproduction or cloning?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — Production of gametes by meiosis (2 marks)
Meiosis produces genetically variable haploid gametes for sexual reproduction. The other options (tissue culture, binary fission, cuttings) all produce genetically identical clones.

options.D: Cuttings being used to grow new plants

subQuestions.questionText: Two related populations of birds become physically separated by a new mountain range. Over many generations they evolve into two species that can no longer interbreed. This is an example of:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — Allopatric speciation (2 marks)
Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are separated by a geographic barrier (here, a mountain range), preventing gene flow and allowing them to diverge into separate species over time.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following is a STOP codon during translation?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — UAA (2 marks)
UAA, UAG, and UGA are the three STOP codons that signal the end of translation. AUG is the START codon (methionine); GCA codes for alanine; CAU codes for histidine.

The diagram shows TWO theories of evolution: A (Lamarck's theory) and B (Darwin's theory of natural selection). Indicate whether each statement (1.4.1 to 1.4.5) applies to A only, B only, BOTH A and B, or NONE.

AUG → Methionine (Met, START) ✓

(b) Cell X (1)

Mark 1: Crossing over — the exchange of equivalent segments of DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to DIAGRAM E (pedigree showing inheritance of haemophilia, a sex-linked recessive disorder, over three generations). State TWO pieces of evidence from the pedigree that support the conclusion that haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive trait.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO points (2 marks):
• All affected individuals in the pedigree are male (II-3, III-2) — typical of sex-linked recessive traits ✓
• The trait skips a generation (carrier mother → unaffected daughter → affected grandson) — typical of recessive inheritance ✓
• An unaffected couple (II-1 × II-2) produces an affected son (III-2) — the parents must both carry the recessive allele, and only the male is affected because the gene is on the X chromosome ✓

(any 2) [2]

Gametes from mother: $X^H$, $X^h$
Gametes from father: $X^H$, $Y$

|   | $X^H$ | $Y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X^H$ | $X^H X^H$ (unaffected female) | $X^H Y$ (unaffected male) |
| $X^h$ | $X^H X^h$ (carrier female) | $X^h Y$ (haemophiliac male) |

Mark 2: Correct offspring genotypes in all four squares ✓
Mark 3: Probability of haemophiliac son = 1/4 = 25% ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why no female in this family is shown as affected by haemophilia, even though the trait is present in the family.
subQuestions.memoText:

Mark 2: This requires an affected father ($X^h Y$) AND a carrier or affected mother — this combination is rare and is not present in this family ✓

Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1978. Show ALL workings.

subQuestions.questionText: Use Darwin's theory of natural selection to explain why this shift in beak depth occurred. Refer specifically to variation, selection pressure, survival and reproduction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any FOUR points for full marks (4 marks):
• Variation — the original 1976 finch population showed variation in beak depth (graph shows a range from ~7 to ~12 mm) ✓
• Selection pressure — the 1977 drought killed small soft seeds; only large, hard seeds remained as food ✓
• Survival of the fittest — finches with deeper, stronger beaks could crack the hard seeds and survived; finches with shallow beaks could not feed and starved ✓
• Reproduction — surviving deep-beaked finches reproduced and passed on the deep-beak alleles to their offspring ✓
• Over generations the proportion of deep-beaked individuals in the population increased, shifting the mean beak depth upward ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to INFORMATION 8 (case study of Hawaiian honeycreepers — over 50 species evolved from a single ancestor on different Hawaiian islands). Identify the type of speciation that has occurred in the Hawaiian honeycreepers and define this term.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Allopatric speciation ✓
Mark 2: The formation of new species from a single ancestral species after populations have been geographically separated/isolated (here, by occupying different islands) so that gene flow between them is prevented ✓
[2]

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the steps by which the original ancestral population evolved into more than 50 modern species. Use full sentences.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A small founder population of finches arrived from North America about 5 mya and dispersed across the Hawaiian islands ✓
Mark 2: Populations on different islands became geographically isolated by sea — gene flow stopped between them ✓
Mark 3: Each island offered different food sources / niches, creating different selection pressures on each population. Over generations, natural selection favoured different beak shapes for the available food on each island ✓
Mark 4: Mutations and accumulated genetic differences between isolated populations led to reproductive isolation — populations could no longer interbreed even if reunited. Each is now a separate species ✓
[4]

subQuestions.questionText: What term is used for the rapid diversification of a single ancestral species into many new species, each adapted to a different niche?

The essay must integrate Darwin's mechanism of natural selection with the case study of antibiotic resistance. It should clearly contrast Darwin's theory with Lamarck's discredited theory of acquired characteristics, and finish with TWO practical actions to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance. Award marks for content as a list of biological points (max 17), then award synthesis marks (max 3) using the rubric.

=== CONTENT MARKS (max 17) ===

(a) Darwin's theory of natural selection (any 4 of these points; max 4 marks):
• Within a population there is natural variation between individuals (caused by mutation, sexual reproduction etc.) ✓
• Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, resulting in competition / struggle for survival ✓
• Some variations make individuals better adapted to their environment than others ✓
• Better-adapted individuals are more likely to survive ('survival of the fittest') and reproduce ✓
• They pass on their favourable alleles to their offspring ✓
• Over many generations the favourable trait becomes more common in the population — the population evolves ✓
(max 4)

(b) Application to antibiotic resistance (any 6 points; max 7 marks):
• In any large bacterial population there is variation: by random mutation a small number of bacteria already carry alleles that make them resistant to a particular antibiotic ✓
• When the antibiotic is administered, it acts as a strong selection pressure on the population ✓
• The vast majority of bacteria (which are non-resistant) are killed by the antibiotic ✓
• The few resistant bacteria survive the antibiotic ✓
• With competing bacteria removed, the resistant bacteria multiply rapidly (every 20 minutes by binary fission), filling the niche left empty by the dead bacteria ✓
• Daughter cells inherit the resistance gene, so within a few generations the entire population is resistant ✓
• The 'superbug' problem is therefore evolution by natural selection happening on a very fast timescale (over weeks/months rather than millennia) ✓
• Resistance can also spread between species via plasmids (horizontal gene transfer), accelerating the problem ✓
(max 7)

(c) Why Lamarck's theory CANNOT explain resistance (any 2 points; max 4 marks):
• Lamarck believed that exposure to a stimulus (e.g. an antibiotic) would cause an organism to acquire resistance during its lifetime, and that this acquired characteristic would be passed on to its offspring ✓
• This is incorrect: the resistance allele was already present by chance mutation BEFORE the antibiotic was applied — exposure merely selected for it; it did not create it ✓
• Acquired characteristics (e.g. damage caused to an organism by an antibiotic) cannot be passed to offspring because they do not alter the DNA in gametes / reproductive cells ✓
• Modern genetics (DNA-based inheritance) supports Darwin and contradicts Lamarck — the cause of resistance is a heritable change in DNA, not an environmentally-induced one ✓
(max 4)

(d) TWO practical actions to slow antibiotic resistance (any 2 actions; max 2 marks):
• Doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when truly necessary (NOT for viral infections such as colds and flu) and prescribe the correct narrow-spectrum drug for the specific bacterium ✓
• Patients must complete the full course of antibiotics, even after they feel better — stopping early leaves the most resistant bacteria alive to multiply ✓
• Hospitals must enforce strict hygiene (handwashing, isolation of infected patients) to prevent the spread of resistant strains ✓
• Reduce the use of antibiotics in the agricultural / livestock industry, where they are often used as growth promoters ✓
• Continued investment in research and development of new antibiotics and alternative therapies ✓
(any 2) (2)

Total content available: 4 + 7 + 4 + 2 = 17 marks (this is the maximum). Award up to a maximum of 17 for content overall.

=== SYNTHESIS MARKS (max 3) ===

3 marks: Excellent overall coherence; logical flow from Darwin's mechanism → application to bacteria → contrast with Lamarck → practical actions; consistent use of correct scientific terminology; ideas linked with cause-and-effect reasoning.

2 marks: Good logical flow with most ideas linked; mostly correct terminology; one or two areas (e.g. the Lamarck contrast or the practical actions) less integrated.

1 mark: Some attempt at flow but ideas mostly listed in disconnected bullet points; limited use of scientific terminology; no clear contrast between Darwin and Lamarck.

0 marks: Disjointed answer; mostly bullet points without explanation; incorrect or absent terminology.

=== TOTALS ===
Maximum content: 17
Maximum synthesis: 3
Maximum essay total: 17 + 3 = 20
